claims.text: The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and the selected equiatomic quaternary and ternary variants are single-phase FCC after identical thermomechanical processing.
The Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni quinary alloy develops pronounced short-range chemical order during deformation.
Deformation-induced short-range order evolves more strongly in the quinary alloy than in its quaternary and ternary subsets.
Evolving short-range chemical order produces heterogeneous local lattice distortions.
The heterogeneous local lattice distortions caused by short-range order impede dislocation motion.
Stronger dislocation pinning increases the yield strength of the quinary alloy.
Stronger dislocation pinning enhances strain hardening in the quinary alloy.
Removing one or two constituents weakens the evolution of short-range chemical order.
Weaker short-range order in the quaternary and ternary alloys permits smoother dislocation motion.
Smoother dislocation motion gives the quaternary and ternary alloys lower mechanical strength than the quinary alloy.
Higher configurational entropy in the quinary alloy promotes dynamic short-range chemical ordering during loading.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will have lower yield strengths.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will have lower strain-hardening rates.
In situ diffraction will show stronger deformation-dependent diffuse scattering in the quinary alloy than in the quaternary and ternary alloys.
Stronger diffuse scattering is an indicator of stronger short-range-order evolution.
Atom probe tomography and high-resolution TEM will reveal more significant atomic-scale ordering or local lattice distortion in the quinary alloy.
Using identical processing, specimen geometry, temperature, and strain rate will make atomic-scale phenomena rather than macroscopic processing variation responsible for observed differences.
The proposed mechanism may not apply at elevated temperatures, high strain rates, or in multiphase materials.
Real-time detection of subtle differences in dynamic short-range-order evolution is experimentally challenging.
Other microstructural phenomena may overlap with and obscure the quantitative relationship between short-range-order-induced lattice distortion and mechanical response.
